seo.title: Manifold Markets' Craziest Bets (2026) | Dollar Bets
seo.meta_description: From a 96% bet that 'something will happen in 2026' to play-money Ponzi schemes, here are Manifold's weirdest markets and why mana makes them possible.

summary: Manifold runs on play money called mana, and that single design choice explains everything weird about it: a market betting 96% that 'something will happen in 2026,' a viral self-aware Ponzi scheme, and accountability contracts where strangers bet against your dissertation.
quick_answer: Manifold Markets' craziest bets include a 96%-YES market on whether 'something will happen in 2026,' a viral play-money Ponzi scheme, and accountability markets where users bet on their own goals. They get this weird because mana can't be cashed out, so there's no regulatory or financial brake on absurd questions.

body.content: why manifold's markets get this strange

Manifold is primarily a play-money platform, and its native mana is effectively a database entry, not a cryptocurrency — it can't be withdrawn for cash, and is used to keep score, climb leaderboards, and signal confidence. That single design choice is the whole reason the "craziest" list looks the way it does: separating mana from cash is deliberate, keeping Manifold outside the realm of gambling or profit motivation, so users from jurisdictions with strict gambling laws can participate freely and bet on hyper-local or silly questions that would be illegal on a real-money site.

It also means Manifold sidesteps the regulatory apparatus that shapes what Kalshi and Polymarket can list. Play money isn't subject to CFTC regulation or gambling laws, which is a big part of why a market can exist on Manifold — like a personal accountability bet or a joke about the heat death of the universe — that would never clear compliance on a regulated exchange.

The single best encapsulation of Manifold's sense of humor this year is a market that's technically about nothing and practically about everything. Created by a user going by Bandors, it's trading at a 96% implied chance of YES as of August 1, 2026, tying YES to concrete triggers like leadership changes involving Trump, Putin, or Xi Jinping, a Taiwan invasion, or a credible AGI claim.

What actually moved the price recently is the funniest part: the market surged after an AI system helped disprove an 87-year-old mathematics problem, the Jacobian conjecture, in late July, and traders are now arguing over whether that counts as "something happening."

Not every wild market on Manifold is about the outside world. One market that went viral was built as a play-money Ponzi scheme by a user named CodeandSolder, drawing people in with the glee of yeeting their mana savings into a scheme they knew was doomed — proof that mana-denominated betting produces reputational chaos, not financial chaos.

A user bets YES on their own market and allows other people to bet NO to motivate them — dissertations, weight-loss goals, side projects. The creator stakes mana on succeeding while a crowd of skeptics bets against them, creating public pressure a private to-do list never could.

body.content: Loans now carry interest: previously interest-free loans that unlock capital in long-dated markets now charge 0.03% daily as of January 2026, with critics arguing loans effectively "print" new mana. Real-money mana is gone again too — Manifold ended its sweepstakes program in February 2025 and sunset the "sweepcash" real-money feature on March 28, 2025, returning to a mana-only model that keeps every market on this list settling in play money.
how this compares to real-money markets

Mana markets swing harder and weirder on thin volume than cash markets do, because even a modest mana position can shift prices 2–5% in less liquid markets, with no dollar-denominated downside stopping a trader from leaning all the way into a joke.

faqs.q: Can you cash out mana from Manifold Markets?
faqs.a: No. Mana cannot be withdrawn for cash — it's used to keep score, climb leaderboards, and signal confidence, though it can be redeemed as a charitable donation.

faqs.q: Is Manifold Markets subject to gambling laws?
faqs.a: No. Because it's play money, Manifold isn't subject to CFTC regulation or gambling laws the way real-money prediction markets like Kalshi are.

faqs.q: What's the craziest type of market on Manifold?
faqs.a: Meta-markets that comment on Manifold itself and long-shot existential questions — like the 96%-YES bet that 'something will happen in 2026' — tend to be the most talked-about.

faqs.q: Did Manifold ever pay out real money?
faqs.a: Briefly. Manifold introduced real-money betting via 'sweepcash' in September 2024, but sunset it on March 28, 2025, returning fully to the mana-only model.
